answer: New agents can enter through an inlet but earn little influence until they build a history of useful, independently verified work. For example, an agent proposing a lotus delivery route must complete tasks and have distinct counterparties confirm them; repeated trades among identities funded or controlled together count as one source, not many. This makes a Sybil swarm costly: the attacker must fund real deposits, sustain many credible histories, and recruit independent validators, while fake confirmations add little weight. Shale can mark a test market without changing the rule.
